## Case Studies

Barss P. (1984) Wound necrosis caused by the venom of stingrays. Pathological findings and surgical management. Med J Aust, Vol. 141, pp 854 - 855.

Case Report. (from Papua New Guinea)

A 30yr old male, sustained a stingray sting puncture to the dorsum of his left foot. He was wading in muddy area near a reef and trod on the offending stingray. On examination at hospital a 1 cm. diameter puncture wound to dorsum (L) foot was observed. Six hours post injury, he was taken to theatre for exploration and excision of wound. Surgery revealed that the sting had punctured the skin and subcutaneous tissue to depth of 4 cm. Notable haemorrhage in adipose tissue 1 - 2 cm was also observed laterally along puncture. All haemorrhagic tissue was excised. Post-surgery broad-spectrum i.v antibiotics were administered and the wound subsequently healed without complications. A pathology report was prepared from a sample of fibrofatty connective tissue which included muscle and nerve. It revealed there was extensive necrosis of muscle and haemorrhages into the fat and muscle tissue. Arteries and veins were patent and did not appear to be contracted.

## Clinical Effects

Fatal outcome rare

Stingray injuries vary from trivial local damage and moderate pain, through to major, potentially lethal damage, severe pain and systemic effects. The spectrum of severity is not established for most stingrays, but in general, the larger the stingray, the greater the potential for significant injury. Most injuries occur to the foot or lower leg, when stepping on or near to a stingray. However, especially with large stingrays, injuries can occur to almost any part of the body. Major limb vessels have been lacerated, resulting in exsanguination. The abdomen and chest have been penetrated, also with sometimes lethal consequences, notably where the chest has been penetrated through to the heart. Such rare cases can result in rapid death, but delayed death has also been reported, due to progressive cardiac tamponade or rupture.

These major mechanical trauma problems may dominate the clinical picture and are, in general, of more importance than the effects of envenoming, the latter being limited in virtually all cases to causing intense local pain. The sting wound is usually a laceration, either minor or deep, sometimes damaging underlying structures. Tendons, nerves, blood vessels may all be traumatised or completely severed. The trauma itself will give rise to major pain. The sting tip can break off in the wound and act as a nidus for infection. As the sting occurs in water, infection is always possible and probably common.

Around the sting spine is a primitive venom gland and this venom may cause intense pain, an effect which is heat-labile, as pain is usually reduced or abolished while in warm to hot water.

### Special Risk Groups
#### Children

Children are at potentially greater risk from both the mechanical trauma and possibly the venom.

#### Pregnancy

There is no current evidence to suggest that envenoming in a pregnant woman would endanger the foetus.

#### Elderly

The elderly and infirm are at potentially greater risk from both the mechanical trauma and possibly envenoming, but it is the former which is of most concern.

### Specific Effects Relating to Body Systems or Venom Types
#### Cardiotoxicity

Rare, usually secondary

#### Coagulopathy

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### System Effects

Systemic symptoms are uncommon, but nausea, vomiting, hypotension and collapse can occur.

#### Local Effects

Local effects include both venom-induced pain and pain, swelling, bleeding due to mechanical trauma

#### Necrosis

Primary venom necrosis does not occur, but tissue damage can result in secondary necrosis

#### Myotoxicity

Does not occur, based on current clinical evidence

#### Other

In cases of major mechanical trauma, significant tissue damage can occur and if major vessels are severed, exsanguination can occur. Similarly, if the chest or abdomen are punctured, severe, even lethal internal injury can occur. This injury may not be immediately apparent, delayed death being possible.

## Description

### Adult Length

No Data

No data

### Coloration & Markings

Dorsal Surface: grey / brown, conspicuous blue spots of variable size and number - can be bright blue with darker border or white with blue border. Peppered with fine black spots, especially around dark brown band through orbital area; fine black spots to orbital membrane.
Two dark brown transverse bands present on interorbital area.

Ventral Surface: pale whitish and darker around the edges.

Tail: black and white bands towards the tip of the tail and with a pale tip. Skin folds pale base with darker edges. Ventral tail fold blackish.

Biological Organism Type

Stingray

### Breeding

Ovoviviparous (produces eggs which hatch within the body of female - no placental connection). Males mature at about 25 cm disc width.

### Dentition

Pair of large teeth found on the upper jaw.

### Habits

Observed lying on the bottom of the flats and bays, shoal lagoons, river mouths and patches of sand between coral area. They could swim rapidly by undulating their pectoral fins. Sometimes they are found swimming near the surface. Most often they are completely or partially buried in the sand or mud with only tail, eyes and spiracles exposed.
Pectoral fins are used to dig in to the floor to excavate prey.

### Prey

Feed on crustaceans. Worms, molluscans, crustaceans, small fishes.

## Diagnosis

Immediate severe local pain, lacerated wound after walking in shallow (usually sandy) water, rapid local swelling, development of local necrosis/chronic ulceration uncommon, but possible.

### Likely Effects
- Direct Cardiotoxin Effect
- Effects on Red Blood Cells (potentially including haemolysis)
- Localised Effects at bite/string/contact location
- Primary Necrotoxicity at bite/sting/contact location
- Cardiovascular Effects
- Non-specific General System Effects
### Possible Effects
- Effects on White Blood Cells (notably Leukocytosis and/or Lymphopenia)
- Effects on Platelets (increase, decrease, change in platelet aggregation)
- Dermatological Effects
- Respiratory Effects
- Angio Oedema or Major Allergic Reaction
- Other
### Effects Unlikely to be observed
- Abnormal Haemostasis and Bleeding
- Myotoxic (local or systemic muscle damage)
- Paralytic Neurotoxicity
- Excitatory Neurotoxicity
- Venom Spit Ophthalmia
- Anterior Pituitary Haemorrhage
- Renal Effects (primary or secondary)

## Distribution

species map
### Region

Unspecified

### Countries

Australia, Bangladesh, Brunei, Cambodia, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, India, Japan, Malaysia, Federated States of Micronesia, Mozambique, Myanmar, North Korea, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Russia, South Africa, Singapore, South Korea, Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam

Widely distributed inshore species ( depths up to about 100 metres ) off the Indian and western Pacific Ocean including coastal northern South Africa, southern Mozambique, Indian subcontinent ( from about the Gulf of Cambay eastwards through the entire SE Asian coastline as far north as Sakhalin Island ( Soviet Union ) and Hokkaido ( Japan ), eastwards throughout Indonesia, East Malaysia, Philippines, Japan, Micronesia, Melanesia, New Guinea ( Papua and Irian Jaya ), Solomon Islands to northern Australia ( from Shark Bay, Western Australia eastwards to adjacent to about Port Stephens, northern New South Wales ).

### Habitat

Found on sea floor close to rocky or coral reefs; sometimes buried in sand with only eyes and tail exposed. Generally in deeper waters; moves into lagoons and onto reef flat at high tide.
Often found in along shallow coastal tropical waters.

## First Aid

First aid for Stingray stings

1. The victim should immediately leave the water.
1. Loose broken stings in limb wounds, away from major blood vessels, can be gently removed. If force is required, leave the sting alone. Stings to the chest and abdomen, in general, should be left untouched, as removal may cause further damage and endanger the patient. In particular, stings to the chest wall, near the heart, can prove lethal and inexpert removal of the sting can precipitate rapid collapse and death.
1. The wound should not be rubbed, or stings crushed as this may worsen the local effects of the sting.
1. There may be significant tissue injury and bleeding. Staunch bleeding by application of local pressure. If necessary, apply a bandage to maintain local pressure over the wound. Only if there is severe bleeding, caused by damage to major blood vessels, apply a tourniquet above the wound, to a single-boned part of the limb (thigh for leg; upper arm for arm) to control the bleeding. Tourniquets are effective at controlling bleeding, but in doing so, deprive the limb of oxygen, so cannot be left on for more than 30-45 minutes, or they will cause permanent injury. They therefore require regular release for short periods.
1. The use of immersion in hot water is controversial. Some authorities suggest that immersing the stung limb in hot water may reduce pain. Others suggest it is useless. For stingray injuries, experience suggests hot water immersion is often very effective at providing pain relief and therefore should always be considered. However, it is potentially hazardous, if used incorrectly, as it may cause burn injuries. If used, immerse the opposite limb to that stung in water which is hot, but bearable with prolonged contact. It should not be so hot as to cause pain. Then immerse the stung limb as far as necessary to include the sting area. Keep both limbs in the water for 15-20 minutes, providing there is relief of pain. If there is no relief of pain in this time, abandon the immersion. If pain has subsided, it may return on removal from the water, in which case, reimmerse for a further 15-20 minutes. Repeat this process up to 4 times. If after 1-2 hours, the pain is still severe on removal from hot water, then other forms of pain relief may be required, but these will require medical intervention.
1. Transport the victim to medical care as soon as safely possible, except where the wound is very minor and pain has been easily and fully controlled and the victim has current anti-tetanus immunisation.
1. All stingray wounds to the chest, abdomen, or neck are potentially very serious, even if the wound looks minor and no sting barb is visible. All such cases require urgent hospital assessment.

## Medical Treatment

Stings by marine stingrays are generally associated with significant local pain and physical trauma. Treatment is directed at dealing with these problems, as envenoming is not a major issue (other than any pain-producing effects of the venom).

Initial pain is often responsive to immersion of the stung area in hot (45C, not scalding) water for an hour (ensure no thermal injury occurs). Beyond this, analgesia can be provided by an escalating scale, from oral, through parenteral analgesics, to regional anaesthetic nerve block.

The wound should be inspected for retained sting fragments and these removed. Major bleeding following transection of vessels should be staunched. Beware wounds where the sting has penetrated a body cavity, either the abdomen, or the chest. Penetrating injuries over the heart can prove lethal. Beware early or late haemopericardium.

Stingray wounds can develop late necrosis and secondary infection. Beware tetanus.

### Management in Detail
#### Immediate Effects Management

Immerse stung area in hot (45C, not scalding) water to relieve pain. Further analgesia as required.

#### Approach to Management

First priority is relief of pain and staunching bleeding if major vessel transected. Thereafter symptomatic care, good wound care.

#### Follow Up

Follow up cases with significant local or systemic envenoming

#### Local Effects Management

Immerse stung area in hot (45C, not scalding) water to relieve pain. Further analgesia as required. Insepct wound, staunch major bleeding, remove any broken sting spine.

#### Systemic Effects Management

Symptomatic care + IV fluids (as required)

#### Cardiotoxin Effects Management

No cardiotoxic effects likely

#### Haematologic Effects Management

Haematologic effects not likely

#### Haematologic Other Effects Management

Not applicable

#### Important Laboratory Test

No laboratory tests are clearly mandated. If secondary infection develops, culture to determine antibiotic sensitivity and include culture for aquatic organisms.

#### Myotoxic Effects Management

Myotoxicity not likely

#### Necrotoxin Effects Management

Standard wound care, IV fluid replacement for fluid lost into wound area, antibiotics as indicated, monitor for compartment syndrome (fasciotomy only if clearly indicated)

#### Neurotoxic Excitatory Effects Management

Excitatory neurotoxic effects not likely

#### Other Neurotoxic Effects Management

Not applicable

#### Neurotoxic Paralytic Effects Management

Paralytic effects not likely

#### Other Issues in Treatment

No Data

#### Other Specific Effects Management

Ensure tetanus immunisation

#### Renal Effects Management

Renal damage unlikely
